Latvia Grapples with Currency Crisis as Lats Plummets, Businesses and Consumers Hit Hard

RIGA – Latvia is facing a severe economic crisis this week as the national currency, the lats, has lost over 30% of its value against the euro and US dollar since late April, sparking fears of widespread financial instability. The rapid depreciation, attributed to a combination of external debt pressures and declining investor confidence, is having swift and sweeping repercussions for Latvian businesses and households.

The crisis began escalating last month after a series of credit rating downgrades and reports of dwindling foreign currency reserves at the Bank of Latvia. Efforts by the central bank to stem the slide, including emergency interest rate hikes to 10% and foreign exchange interventions, have so far failed to halt the lats’ fall.

"Import costs have surged almost overnight," said Liga Ozolina, head of the Latvian Retailers Association. "Food, fuel, and electronics prices are rising sharply, and we expect further increases in the coming weeks." Retailers report that wholesale prices for imported goods have jumped by 25% on average since the start of May.

Manufacturers are also feeling the pain. Andris Kalnins, CFO at the electronics firm DatiWorks, noted, "Many of our components come from abroad. With the lats so weak, our input costs have soared, and we’re struggling to maintain margins."

The crisis has stoked anxiety among consumers, with banks reporting a surge in withdrawals and long lines at currency exchange offices. “People are worried about their savings losing value,” said Inese Jansone, an economist at the Riga Institute for Economic Studies. “Confidence in the lats is at an all-time low.”

The Latvian government has pledged to protect depositors and is reportedly in talks with the International Monetary Fund for emergency assistance. Finance Minister Edgars Briedis said in a statement on Thursday, "We are deploying all available tools to stabilize the currency and ensure the safety of the banking sector. Our priority is to limit the impact on ordinary Latvians and safeguard jobs."

Unions have warned of potential layoffs if the crisis persists. “If the lats continues to weaken, we will see job cuts across manufacturing, retail, and logistics,” predicted Janis Vilks, spokesperson for the Latvian Workers’ Federation.

As the situation develops, analysts warn that without swift external support and decisive policy action, Latvia could face a prolonged downturn, with ripple effects across the Baltic region.
